around: ng El Niño By Nash Villena No Comments 2 Mins Read October 28, 2026 7:17 pm Share this Article Metro Manila, Philippines – The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) released a labor advisory on Tuesday, Oct. 27, outlining safety protocols for workers in times of extreme heat. Labor Advisory No. 20 seeks to guide employers in safeguarding their workers from heat-related illnesses due to the ongoing El Niño event. Employers are required to conduct and document hazard and risk assessments to address heat stress and El Niño-related workplace risks. They should also monitor weather conditions, heat index data, and five-day heat index forecasts. The DOLE also directed employers to ensure compliance with government contributions and track work-related heat illnesses in medical logs and annual medical reports. In addition, the Labor Department provided heat index-based guidelines for employers ranging from caution to extreme danger levels. Caution level heat index (27°C–32°C) requires the availability of safe drinking water, ventilated break spots, and regular hydration among workers; extreme caution level (33°C–41°C) entails routine rest and the supply of appropriate protective gear; danger level (42°C–51°C) prompts the implementation of flexible work arrangements to limit heat exposure; and extreme danger levels (52°C and higher) necessitate re-evaluation of tasks and possible rescheduling or work relocation. Last week, DOLE issued Labor Advisory No. 19, centered on workers’ compensation for heat-related illnesses. phla-sunstar.title: DOLE: Heat-Sick Workers May Get Compensation Amid El Niño
around: id. El Niño in Cebu In Cebu, the province is experiencing the effects of a strong to very strong El Niño, with drier conditions expected in the coming months. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) Visayas earlier said Cebu may experience below-normal to way-below-normal rainfall from November 2026 to March 2027, while drought conditions may develop from January to March. The dry conditions could persist until June 2027, depending on how El Niño develops. Who is covered The guidelines apply to outdoor and indoor workers who are covered by the Employees’ Compensation Program (ECP) through the Social Security System and the Government Service Insurance System, and who are exposed, or may reasonably be expected to be exposed, to excessive heat at work. Heat stroke, heat cramps and heat exhaustion remain compensable under existing ECP rules. Other heat-related illnesses may also qualify, including heat syncope (fainting and dizziness), heat rash (bungang araw), rhabdomyolysis (muscle damage), neurological disorders that affect normal nervous system function and dehydration that leads to kidney injury. Proving the link To determine whether an illness is work-related, authorities may consider the nature of the worker’s job, workplace conditions, duration and intensity of heat exposure, protective clothing and equipment, preventive measures and other relevant circumstances. Pagasa’s heat index classifications may be used as supporting evidence of workplace heat conditions. Employer duties Dole requires employers to keep records of work-related heat illnesses and to help affected workers or their beneficiaries file compensation claims. Records that may support a claim include occupational safety and health documents, workplace temperature measurements, work schedules, physical workload and work-rest arrangements, preventive measures and witness statements. Employers must also follow existing reporting rules, including submitting a Work Accident/Illness Report when required. The Employees’ Compensation Commission, through its Regional Extension Units, and Dole regional offices and attached agencies will provide technical assistance in implementing the guidelines. Employers, workers, unions, safety and health committees, and occupational safety and health personnel are encouraged to strengthen measures against heat-related illnesses, report incidents and arrange medical referrals. / DPC Show Comments Trending 27-storey tower planned for Larsian Katlene O. The advisory covers private-sector employers and workers and calls for workplace-specific assessments of heat-related risks, including those caused by water shortages, power interruptions, and reduced ventilation or cooling. The advisory outlines measures based on heat-risk levels, including providing safe drinking water and suitable rest areas, setting work-rest schedules, and moving strenuous tasks to cooler hours. Flexible work arrangements may be used when heat exposure is high, while work may need to be suspended, relocated, or rescheduled if serious risks cannot be adequately controlled. Employers are also expected to prepare for heat-related emergencies, while workers should follow safety measures and promptly report symptoms or unsafe conditions.
